The following snippet of code will allow you to rename or adjust your subverse's displayed name. For instance, I used it to put capital letters and spaces in between words for /v/BobRoss and /v/OldTimeRadio. Please note these changes are only to the CSS displayed so anyone who disables custom subverse styles will still see the original subverse name. This also does not effect your subverse's url so you still have to type/use the original address if creating a link to it.

Also this only changes the name at the top of your subverse. The name displayed in the sidebar is unchanged. I'll be working on that one shortly.

/*=====RENAME THE SUBVERSE=====*/
.pagename a:after,
.titlebox .voatname a:after {
 content: "Your Subverse Name"; /* type the custom name here */
}

.pagename a, .titlebox .voatname a {
 font-size: 0!important;
}

 .pagename a:after {
 font-size: 18px;
 vertical-align: bottom;
 }

Please let me know if you like these tips and find them helpful.

Nothing but contempt for these two corporate lackeys attempting to delay the vote under the guise of caring about "the future of the internet." They've sold out their constituents and their country.

While it's certainly an unorthodox request for the FCC, I don't consider it to be a bad idea. Federal governmental agencies have a "notice and comment" period, within which, as the title suggests, they provide notice to the public of their proposed policy and give the people some time to comment on it, suggesting changes, etc.

There's a reason this is the general scheme: it helps put a democratic check on an otherwise undemocratic agency whose members are all appointed by the President. While the FCC has already received many such comments on this issue, I personally wouldn't mind a a few more going in before the rules are imposed on the rest of us, especially given the particularly sordid history of utilities regulations backfiring.

The previous comments period was more than sufficient, unless you believe the telecoms are going to astroturf more convincingly this time around. The overwhelming consensus was that these rules are a positive thing. To claim this additional comment period is anything but a delaying tactic is just disingenuous.

It's clearly a delay tactic, but I don't mind delaying the imposition of entirely new regulations which contain complex issues and attempt to regulate a whole new set of services.

Regulation in general is a tool to be used only when serious problems exist in an industry that cannot or will not go away on their own. Net neutrality, nice as it sounds when phrased that way, is by contrast a preemptive regulation seeking to "solve" problems that, for the most part, don't even exist yet. Especially given the history we have of well-intentioned regulations causing more problems than they solved, we should be particularly hesitant here and make sure that it's done right, if it must be done at all.
Am I the only one scared to death of the federal government getting involved in the internet?
